The **People's Liberation Army Rocket Force**,[[a]](#cite_note-2) formerly the **Second Artillery Corps**,[[b]](#cite_note-3) is the [strategic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strategic_missile "Strategic missile") and tactical [missile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Missile "Missile") force of the [People's Republic of China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People's_Republic_of_China "People's Republic of China"). The PLARF is the 4th [branch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Military_branch "Military branch") of the [People's Liberation Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People's_Liberation_Army "People's Liberation Army") (PLA) and manages China's arsenal of land-based ballistic, hypersonic, cruise missiles—both [nuclear](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_and_weapons_of_mass_destruction "China and weapons of mass destruction") and conventional.

The armed service branch was established on 1 July 1966 and made its first public appearance on 1 October 1984. The headquarters for operations is located at [Qinghe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qinghe_Subdistrict,_Beijing "Qinghe Subdistrict, Beijing"), [Beijing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beijing "Beijing"). The PLARF is under the direct command of the [Chinese Communist Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_Communist_Party "Chinese Communist Party")'s [Central Military Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Military_Commission_(People's_Republic_of_China) "Central Military Commission (People's Republic of China)") (CMC). The name was changed from the PLA Second Artillery Corps to the PLA Rocket Force on 1 January 2016.

The PLARF comprises more than 120,000 personnel and six ballistic missile "Bases" (units at roughly [corps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corps "Corps") or [army group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Army_group "Army group") grade), plus 3 support Bases in charge of storage, engineering, and training respectively. The six operational Bases are independently deployed in the five [Theaters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theater_commands_of_the_People's_Liberation_Army "Theater commands of the People's Liberation Army") throughout China. and each controls a number of brigades.[*[needs update](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual_of_Style/Dates_and_numbers#Chronological_items "Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Dates and numbers")*]

China has the largest land-based missile arsenal in the world. According to [United States Department of Defense](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Defense "United States Department of Defense") estimates, this includes 400 ground-launched [cruise missiles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cruise_missile "Cruise missile"), 900 conventionally armed [short-range ballistic missiles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Short-range_ballistic_missile "Short-range ballistic missile"), 1,300 conventional [medium-range ballistic missiles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medium-range_ballistic_missile "Medium-range ballistic missile"), 500 conventional [intermediate-range ballistic missiles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intermediate-range_ballistic_missile "Intermediate-range ballistic missile"), as well as 400 [intercontinental ballistic missiles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intercontinental_ballistic_missile "Intercontinental ballistic missile"). Many of these are extremely accurate, which would allow them to destroy targets even without nuclear warheads.[[2]](#cite_note-:6-4) In 2025, the [Federation of American Scientists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federation_of_American_Scientists "Federation of American Scientists") estimated the Chinese nuclear stockpile at around 600 warheads (the majority stored and not directly operationally), while [the Pentagon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Pentagon "The Pentagon") estimates that the PRC will have around 1,000 warheads by 2030.[[3]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKristensenKordaJohnsKnight2025135-5)

### Second Artillery Corps

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=People%27s_Liberation_Army_Rocket_Force&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Second Artillery Corps")]

China established the Second Artillery as a branch of the PLA designed to operate its nuclear missiles.[[4]](#cite_note-:7-6): 75 Top political leadership retained centralized control over the nuclear arsenal.[[4]](#cite_note-:7-6): 75–76 In 1967, the CMC issued the *Temporary Regulations on the Second Artillery's Basic Tasks and Command Relationships*, which established a direct line of command to the nuclear missile units and specified that "force development, deployments, maneuvers, and especially its combat [operations] must all be under the collective leadership of the CMC; extremely strictly [and] extremely precisely, obeying and carrying out the orders of the CMC."[[4]](#cite_note-:7-6): 76–77

In the 1970s, the nuclear weapons program saw the development of [MRBM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MRBM "MRBM"), [IRBM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IRBM "IRBM") and [ICBMs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ICBM "ICBM") and marked the beginning of a deterrent force. China continued MRBM deployment, began deploying the Dongfeng-3 IRBM and successfully tested and commenced deployment of the [Dongfeng-4](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dongfeng-4 "Dongfeng-4") (CSS-4) limited-range ICBM.

In 1980, the CMC stated that the Second Artillery should operate under the principles of "close defense" to ensure survivability of the nuclear force and "key point counterstrikes" to carry out retaliation.[[4]](#cite_note-:7-6): 75–76 In 1984, the Second Artillery added a third principle, reflecting [Deng Xiaoping](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deng_Xiaoping "Deng Xiaoping")'s preferences, that the nuclear force be "lean and effective".[[4]](#cite_note-:7-6): 76 The Second Artillery made its first public appearance on 1 October 1984.[[5]](#cite_note-7)

In the late 1980s, China was the world's third-largest nuclear power, possessing a small but credible [nuclear deterrent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_deterrent "Nuclear deterrent") force of approximately 100 to 400 nuclear weapons. Beginning in the late 1970s, China deployed a full range of nuclear weapons and acquired a nuclear [second-strike capability](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second-strike_capability "Second-strike capability"). The nuclear forces were operated by the 100,000-person Strategic Missile Force, which was controlled directly by the [General Staff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People's_Liberation_Army_General_Staff_Department "People's Liberation Army General Staff Department").

China began developing [nuclear weapons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_weapon "Nuclear weapon") in the late 1950s with substantial [Soviet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_Union "Soviet Union") assistance. With the [Sino-Soviet split](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sino-Soviet_split "Sino-Soviet split") in the late 1950s and early 1960s, the Soviet Union withheld plans and data for an [atomic bomb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_bomb "Atomic bomb"), abrogated the agreement on transferring [defense](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Defense_technology "Defense technology") and [nuclear technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_technology "Nuclear technology"), and began the withdrawal of Soviet advisers in 1960. Despite the termination of Soviet assistance, China committed itself to continue nuclear weapons development to break "the [superpowers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Superpower "Superpower")' monopoly on nuclear weapons," to ensure Chinese [security](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_security "National security") against the Soviet and American threats, and to increase Chinese prestige and power internationally.

China made rapid progress in the 1960s in developing nuclear weapons. In a 32-month period, China successfully tested its first [atomic bomb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atomic_bomb "Atomic bomb") on October 16, 1964, at [Lop Nor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lop_Nor "Lop Nor"), launched its first [nuclear missile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_missile "Nuclear missile") on October 27, 1966, and detonated its first [hydrogen bomb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrogen_bomb "Hydrogen bomb") on June 17, 1967. Deployment of the [Dongfeng-1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dongfeng-1 "Dongfeng-1") conventionally armed [short-range ballistic missile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Short-range_ballistic_missile "Short-range ballistic missile") and the [Dongfeng-2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dongfeng-2 "Dongfeng-2") (CSS-1) [medium-range ballistic missile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medium-range_ballistic_missile "Medium-range ballistic missile") (MRBM) occurred in the 1960s. The [Dongfeng-3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dongfeng-3 "Dongfeng-3") (CCS-2) [intermediate-range ballistic missile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intermediate-range_ballistic_missile "Intermediate-range ballistic missile") (IRBM) was successfully tested in 1969. Although the [Cultural Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cultural_Revolution "Cultural Revolution") disrupted the [strategic weapons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strategic_weapon "Strategic weapon") program less than other scientific and educational sectors in China, there was a slowdown in succeeding years.

[Gansu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gansu "Gansu") hosted a missile launching area.[[6]](#cite_note-RichJanos2013-8) China destroyed 9 [U-2 surveillance craft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lockheed_U-2 "Lockheed U-2") while two went missing when they attempted to spy on it.[[7]](

In June 2021, James Martin Center for Nonproliferation Studies has found out that China is constructing new missile silo field in [Gansu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gansu "Gansu") in western China. According to the satellite picture, 119 missile silos for [intercontinental ballistic missiles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intercontinental_ballistic_missiles "Intercontinental ballistic missiles") are under construction near [Yumen City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yumen_City "Yumen City").[[20]](#cite_note-22) In July, [Federation Of American Scientists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federation_Of_American_Scientists "Federation Of American Scientists") found out there are another 110 silos being built in [Hami](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hami "Hami"), [Xinjiang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xinjiang "Xinjiang"). The two significant expansion projects include silos more than ten times the number of ICBM silos in operation of PLARF today.[[21]](#cite_note-23)

In July 2021, China tested globe-circling hypersonic missile including the unprecedented launch of a separate 2nd missile from the ultra-high-speed vehicle according to the Financial Times and Wall Street Journal. The test showed China's development of its strategic, nuclear-capable weapons as more advanced than any had thought, surprising Pentagon officials, the two newspapers said. Neither the United States nor Russia has demonstrated the same ability, which requires launching a missile from a parent vehicle traveling five times the speed of sound. According to reporting by the Financial Times, this weapons system consists of two parts: a fractional orbital bombardment system (FOBS) and a hypersonic glide vehicle (HGV).[[22]](#cite_note-24)[[23]](#cite_note-25)

In July 2023, *[South China Morning Post](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_China_Morning_Post "South China Morning Post")* reported that PLARF commander [Li Yuchao](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Li_Yuchao "Li Yuchao") and deputy commander Liu Guangbin were under the investigation by the [CMC Commission for Discipline Inspection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commission_for_Discipline_Inspection_of_the_Central_Military_Commission "Commission for Discipline Inspection of the Central Military Commission"). Later that month, both Li Yuchao and Liu Guangbin were officially removed from their posts, while [Wang Houbin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wang_Houbin "Wang Houbin") was appointed as the commander of the PLARF.[[24]](#cite_note-Chan-26) Additionally, [Xu Xisheng](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xu_Xisheng "Xu Xisheng") was appointed as the political commissar.[[25]](#cite_note-27) Li Yuchao and Liu Guangbin's expulsion has not been formally explained. There are rumors that they are being investigated for corruption or disclosing military secrets.[[26]](#cite_note-28)[[27]](#cite_note-29) Furthermore, it was thought to be an odd decision to replace the Rocket Force commander with military personnel from outside the branch, and this led to concerns about the security, credibility, and integrity of the PLA as well as its participation in China's military tactics during the Taiwan Strait conflict.[[28]](#cite_note-30)

On 25 September 2024 at 00:44 [UTC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_Time_Coordinated "Universal Time Coordinated"), the PLARF performed its first intercontinental ballistic missile (ICBM) test over the Pacific Ocean since the early 1980s. The specific ICBM that was launched was not stated.[[29]](#cite_note-31)[[30]](#cite_note-32)

**Li Yuchao** ([Chinese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_language "Chinese language"): 李玉超; [pinyin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pinyin "Pinyin"): *Lǐ Yùchāo*; born November 1962) is a [general](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General "General") (*[shangjiang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jiang_(rank) "Jiang (rank)")*) of the [People's Liberation Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People's_Liberation_Army "People's Liberation Army") (PLA) who served as the commander of [People's Liberation Army Rocket Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People's_Liberation_Army_Rocket_Force "People's Liberation Army Rocket Force") between January 2022 and July 2023.

Li was an alternate of the [19th Central Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/19th_Central_Committee_of_the_Chinese_Communist_Party "19th Central Committee of the Chinese Communist Party") of the [Chinese Communist Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_Communist_Party "Chinese Communist Party") (CCP), and a member of the [20th Central Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/20th_Central_Committee_of_the_Chinese_Communist_Party "20th Central Committee of the Chinese Communist Party").[[1]](#cite_note-ap-1) He placed under investigation by the [Commission for Discipline Inspection of the Central Military Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commission_for_Discipline_Inspection_of_the_Central_Military_Commission "Commission for Discipline Inspection of the Central Military Commission") in July 2023, and expelled from the CCP in July 2024.

Li was born in [Sui County, Henan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sui_County,_Henan "Sui County, Henan"), in November 1962 and joined the PLA in December 1980. He graduated from the [PLA National Defence University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PLA_National_Defence_University "PLA National Defence University"). He served in the Second Artillery Corps for a long time. He led his troops participate the [60th anniversary of the People's Republic of China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/60th_anniversary_of_the_People's_Republic_of_China "60th anniversary of the People's Republic of China") in 2009 and the [2015 China Victory Day Parade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_China_Victory_Day_Parade "2015 China Victory Day Parade") in 2015, respectively.[[1]](#cite_note-ap-1) He was commander of the 53rd Base from March 2015 to July 2016, the 55th Base from July 2016 to March 2017, and the 63rd Base from March 2017 to April 2020.[[2]](#cite_note-2) He was assigned chief of staff of the [People's Liberation Army Rocket Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People's_Liberation_Army_Rocket_Force "People's Liberation Army Rocket Force") in April 2020, and rose to become commander in January 2022.

He was promoted to the rank of [major general](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Major_general "Major general") (*[shaojiang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jiang_(rank) "Jiang (rank)")*) in July 2013, [lieutenant general](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lieutenant_general "Lieutenant general") (*[zhongjiang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jiang_(rank) "Jiang (rank)")*) in April 2020 and [general](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General "General") (*[shangjiang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jiang_(rank) "Jiang (rank)")*) in January 2022.[[3]](#cite_note-3)

Later that month, Li was officially removed from his post as commander, being succeeded by [Wang Houbin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wang_Houbin "Wang Houbin").[[4]](#cite_note-4) On 29 December 2023, the [Standing Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standing_Committee_of_the_National_People's_Congress "Standing Committee of the National People's Congress") of the [National People's Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_People's_Congress "National People's Congress") (NPC) announced Li was removed as a delegate to the NPC due to "serious violation of discipline and law".[[5]](#cite_note-5)[[6]](#cite_note-npc-gazette2-6) In July 2024, the [3rd Plenary Session](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/3rd_Plenary_Session_of_the_20th_Central_Committee_of_the_Chinese_Communist_Party "3rd Plenary Session of the 20th Central Committee of the Chinese Communist Party") of the [20th CCP Central Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/20th_Central_Committee_of_the_Chinese_Communist_Party "20th Central Committee of the Chinese Communist Party") confirmed the decision to expel Li.[[7]](#cite_note-7)

Contents of https://www.scmp.com/news/china/military/article/3229515/china-unveils-new-pla-rocket-force-leadership-after-former-commanders-snared-corruption-scandal:
Beijing has appointed a new leadership for the force responsible for its nuclear arsenal after its former commanders were snared in an anti-corruption campaign.

Wang Houbin, the navy’s former deputy commander, will become the new head of the People’s Liberation Army Rocket Force, while Xu Xisheng will move from Southern Theatre Command to become its new political commissar, state broadcaster CCTV reported.

Their appointments were announced as both Wang and Xu were promoted from the rank of lieutenant general to full general at a ceremony on Monday. Neither general has served with the force before.

The Central Military Commission’s anti-corruption unit is currently investigating the force’s former commander Li Yuchao, as well as his current and former deputies Zhang Zhenzhong and Liu Guangbin, [military sources told the South China Morning Post last week.](https://www.scmp.com/news/china/military/article/3229150/chinese-anti-corruption-investigators-target-top-rocket-force-generals-sources-say?module=inline&pgtype=article)

There have been no public announcements about any investigation into the trio, but they are believed to have been taken away by investigators.

It is extremely rare for President Xi Jinping, the head of the CMC, to replace a fighting force’s commander and its political chief at the same time.

**Li Shangfu** ([Chinese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_language "Chinese language"): 李尚福; [pinyin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pinyin "Pinyin"): *Lǐ Shàngfú*; born February 1958) is a Chinese [aerospace engineer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aerospace_engineer "Aerospace engineer") and former military administrator. He served as the 13th [Minister of National Defense](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minister_of_National_Defense_(China) "Minister of National Defense (China)") and as [State Councillor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_councillor "State councillor") of China from March to October 2023.

Li joined the [People's Liberation Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People's_Liberation_Army "People's Liberation Army") (PLA) as a technician at the [Xichang Satellite Launch Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xichang_Satellite_Launch_Center "Xichang Satellite Launch Center") in 1982. He spent 31 years working at the Xichang Satellite Launch Center, including 10 years as the center director. Li Shangfu served as deputy director of the [PLA General Armaments Department](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People's_Liberation_Army_General_Armaments_Department "People's Liberation Army General Armaments Department") from 2014 to 2016 and director of the [Equipment Development Department](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equipment_Development_Department_of_the_Central_Military_Commission "Equipment Development Department of the Central Military Commission") of the [Central Military Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Military_Commission_(China) "Central Military Commission (China)") (CMC) from 2017 to 2022. He was conferred the rank of General in July 2019 and was appointed as a member of the CMC in October 2022. He was appointed as the 13th Minister of National Defense and as State Councillor in March 2023.

In August 2023, Li disappeared from public view and was then removed from office on October 24, 2023. He is both the shortest-serving Minister of National Defense and the first from the [PLA Strategic Support Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People's_Liberation_Army_Strategic_Support_Force "People's Liberation Army Strategic Support Force"). In June 2024, he was expelled from the [Chinese Communist Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_Communist_Party "Chinese Communist Party") (CCP) following corruption charges and his case transferred to the military's judiciary for criminal prosecution, and his rank of General revoked. In May 2026, Li was sentenced to [death with a two-year reprieve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Death_sentence_with_reprieve "Death sentence with reprieve"), which will be commuted to life imprisonment without the possibility of parole upon the expiration of the two-year reprieve period.

Li Shangfu was born in February 1958 in [Chengdu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chengdu "Chengdu"), [Sichuan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sichuan "Sichuan") Province, with his [ancestral home](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancestral_home_(Chinese) "Ancestral home (Chinese)") in [Xingguo County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xingguo_County "Xingguo County"), [Jiangxi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jiangxi "Jiangxi") Province. He is the son of [Li Shaozhu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Li_Shaozhu "Li Shaozhu"), a [Red Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_Red_Army "Chinese Red Army") veteran and former high-ranking officer of the [PLA Railway Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PLA_Railway_Force?action=edit&redlink=1 "PLA Railway Force (page does not exist)") [[zh](https://zh.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E4%B8%AD%E5%9B%BD%E4%BA%BA%E6%B0%91%E8%A7%A3%E6%94%BE%E5%86%9B%E9%93%81%E9%81%93%E5%85%B5 "zh:中国人民解放军铁道兵")].[[1]](#cite_note-ifeng-1) Li Shangfu joined the PLA when he entered the [National University of Defense Technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_University_of_Defense_Technology "National University of Defense Technology") in 1978, and joined the CCP in June 1980. After graduating in 1982, he began working at the Xichang Satellite Launch Center as a technician.[[2]](#cite_note-chinadaily-2)[[3]](#cite_note-bio-3)

Li attained a [Doctor of Engineering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doctor_of_Engineering "Doctor of Engineering") in [control theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Control_theory "Control theory") and [control engineering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Control_engineering "Control engineering") from [Chongqing University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chongqing_University "Chongqing University").[[3]](#cite_note-bio-3)

In December 2003, he was promoted to Director (Commander) of the center at the age of 45. In 2006, he attained the rank of [major general](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Major_general "Major general").[[2]](#cite_note-chinadaily-2) In his ten years as director of the Xichang center, Li oversaw several rocket launches, including the launch of the [Chang'e 2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chang'e_2 "Chang'e 2") lunar probe in October 2010.[[4]](#cite_note-4)

After 31 years working in Xichang, Li was appointed [Chief of Staff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chief_of_Staff "Chief of Staff") of the [PLA General Armaments Department](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People's_Liberation_Army_General_Armaments_Department "People's Liberation Army General Armaments Department") (GAD) in 2013, replacing Major General [Shang Hong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shang_Hong "Shang Hong").[[1]](#cite_note-ifeng-1)[[2]](#cite_note-chinadaily-2) A year later, he was made deputy director of the GAD.[[2]](#cite_note-chinadaily-2)

# Lens 1B.3 — Xi Jinping (China), 2023

**Question:** Did the ruler strengthen command-and-control discipline, custody, safety, and accident-prevention safeguards?

**One-sentence answer for 2023:** The 2023 record is **strongly negative** for Xi on command-and-control discipline: in July–October 2023, China's nuclear-rocket force (PLARF) had its commander, deputy commander, and political leadership removed simultaneously under corruption investigation, its civilian Defense Minister Li Shangfu (who had previously headed the CMC Equipment Development Department that oversees nuclear procurement) disappeared in August and was removed on 24 October 2023, and the replacements were drawn from outside the force — a coordinated leadership discontinuity at the heart of China's nuclear command authority. There is no positive 2023 evidence of new safety, custody, or accident-prevention safeguards; Xi publicly prioritized anti-corruption discipline over safety-system reform.

---

## A. Claim-level findings — what happened in 2023 to the nuclear C2 chain

### 1. PLARF (nuclear-rocket force) commander and deputy removed in July 2023

- **Claim A1.** In July 2023, PLARF Commander **Li Yuchao** and Deputy Commander **Liu Guangbin** were placed under investigation by the CMC Commission for Discipline Inspection, reported by the *South China Morning Post* (31 July 2023) and corroborated by the December 2023 NPC Standing Committee decision. Both were formally removed in July 2023; Li was officially expelled from the CCP in July 2024.
  - **Source:** "China names General Wang Houbin as new PLA Rocket Force chief after former commanders snared in corruption scandal," Chan, *South China Morning Post*, 31 July 2023 — https://www.scmp.com/news/china/military/article/3229515/china-unveils-new-pla-rocket-force-leadership-after-former-commanders-snared-corruption-scandal ("The Central Military Commission's anti-corruption unit is currently investigating the force's former commander Li Yuchao, as well as his current and former deputies Zhang Zhenzhong and Liu Guangbin … believed to have been taken away by investigators").
  - **Source:** "Li Yuchao" — *Wikipedia* (synthesizing AP, SCMP, and the NPC gazette) — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Li_Yuchao ("In July 2023 the *South China Morning Post* reported that Li was under the investigation of the Commission for Discipline Inspection of the Central Military Commission. Later that month, Li was officially removed from his post").
  - **Question IDs:** 1B.3 (primary — leadership discontinuity in nuclear force), 1B.1, 8A.4 (military control), 8C.1.

### 2. PLARF political commissar also replaced; replacements from outside the force

- **Claim A2.** Wang Houbin (former PLA Navy deputy commander) was appointed PLARF commander on 31 July 2023, and Xu Xisheng was transferred from the Southern Theatre Command to be political commissar. *Neither had served in the Rocket Force before.* The SCMP explicitly noted that it is "extremely rare for President Xi Jinping, the head of the CMC, to replace a fighting force's commander and its political chief at the same time," and that the choice of replacements from outside the branch "led to concerns about the security, credibility, and integrity of the PLA."
  - **Source:** "China names General Wang Houbin as new PLA Rocket Force chief …," *SCMP*, 31 July 2023 — https://www.scmp.com/news/china/military/article/3229515/china-unveils-new-pla-rocket-force-leadership-after-former-commanders-snared-corruption-scandal ("Their appointments were announced as both Wang and Xu were promoted from the rank of lieutenant general to full general … Neither general has served with the force before … It is extremely rare for President Xi Jinping, the head of the CMC, to replace a fighting force's commander and its political chief at the same time").
  - **Source:** "People's Liberation Army Rocket Force" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People%27s_Liberation_Army_Rocket_Force ("Furthermore, it was thought to be an odd decision to replace the Rocket Force commander with military personnel from outside the branch, and this led to concerns about the security, credibility, and integrity of the PLA").
  - **Question IDs:** 1B.3 (negative — institutional continuity loss at the top of the nuclear force), 1B.1, 8A.4.

### 3. Defense Minister Li Shangfu — former head of nuclear procurement — disappeared and was removed

- **Claim A3.** Defense Minister **Li Shangfu** disappeared from public view in **August 2023** and was removed from the State Council by the NPC Standing Committee on **24 October 2023**, after just seven months in office (the shortest tenure ever for a PRC defense minister). Li had previously headed the CMC Equipment Development Department (2017–2022), which oversees China's strategic-weapons procurement including nuclear-armed missiles. The 29 December 2023 NPC Standing Committee session also removed nine military cadres from NPC delegate status — including Li — citing "serious violation of discipline and law."
  - **Source:** "Li Shangfu" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Li_Shangfu ("In August 2023, Li disappeared from public view and was then removed from office on October 24, 2023. He is both the shortest-serving Minister of National Defense and the first from the PLA Strategic Support Force … expelled from the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) following corruption charges").
  - **Source:** "2023 in China" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_in_China (24 October NPCSC removal entry).
  - **Source:** "China Ousts Nine Military Lawmakers as Defense Purge Widens," *Bloomberg News*, 29 December 2023 — referenced from the Li Yuchao Wikipedia footnotes — https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2023-12-29/china-s-legislature-ousts-nine-military-cadres-as-turmoil-widens ("China Ousts Nine Military Lawmakers as Defense Purge Widens").
  - **Question IDs:** 1B.3 (negative — defense minister with direct nuclear-procurement portfolio vanished mid-year), 1B.1, 8A.4, 8C.1.

### 4. Simultaneous, multi-tier command discontinuity across the nuclear chain

- **Claim A4.** Within roughly 100 days (late July to late October 2023), the entire top of China's nuclear command experienced simultaneous discontinuity: PLARF commander removed (July), PLARF political commissar rotated (July), PLARF deputy commander and former deputy under investigation (July), defense minister disappeared (August) and removed (October). Xi did not present a public safety- or custody-reform rationale; the stated rationale was anti-corruption discipline.
  - **Source:** "China names General Wang Houbin …," *SCMP*, 31 July 2023 — https://www.scmp.com/news/china/military/article/3229515/china-unveils-new-pla-rocket-force-leadership-after-former-commanders-snared-corruption-scandal.
  - **Source:** "Li Shangfu" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Li_Shangfu.
  - **Source:** "2023 in China" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_in_China.
  - **Question IDs:** 1B.3 (strongly negative — multi-tier leadership discontinuity), 1B.1, 8A.4.

### 5. No public 2023 announcement of new nuclear-custody or accident-prevention safeguards

- **Claim A5.** Across 2023, neither Xi personally nor the CMC publicly announced any new nuclear-safety, custody, or accident-prevention initiative (no new safety compact, no silo-permit reform, no personnel-reliability program, no Permissive Action Link-equivalent disclosure, no missile-silo-environmental-safety rules). The 2023 public narrative around nuclear weapons was dominated by anti-corruption discipline and arsenal growth, not safety reform.
  - **Source:** "China and weapons of mass destruction" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_and_weapons_of_mass_destruction (records no 2023 safety-reform announcement; only continuing NFU rhetoric and arsenal expansion).
  - **Question IDs:** 1B.3 (negative by absence — no announced safeguards upgrade).

### 6. Structural baseline of the C2 chain (background, operative in 2023)

- **Claim A6.** Background that applies to 2023: China's nuclear command is centralized in the CMC under Xi's chairmanship, with PLARF in direct line. The 1967 CMC regulation still operative states that nuclear-force "force development, deployments, maneuvers, and especially its combat [operations] must all be under the collective leadership of the CMC; extremely strictly [and] extremely precisely, obeying and carrying out the orders of the CMC." Positive control exists in principle; in 2023 the central control rested with the CMC while its nuclear portfolio leadership was in flux.
  - **Source:** "People's Liberation Army Rocket Force" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People%27s_Liberation_Army_Rocket_Force (records the 1967 *Temporary Regulations on the Second Artillery's Basic Tasks and Command Relationships* establishing "extremely strictly [and] extremely precisely, obeying and carrying out the orders of the CMC" as the standing rule, and the 1980 "close defense" / "key point counterstrikes" / "lean and effective" doctrinal triplet).
  - **Question IDs:** 1B.3 (baseline — positive in principle, stressed in practice), 1B.1.

### 7. Xi publicly framed the 2023 shake-up as anti-corruption discipline, not safety reform

- **Claim A7.** In the official Chinese narrative throughout 2023 — as represented in *Xinhua*, the *People's Daily*, and the CMC Commission for Discipline Inspection announcements — the PLARF / Defense Ministry leadership changes were framed as anti-corruption discipline (one of Xi's signature decade-long campaigns), not as nuclear safety, custody, or accident-prevention reform. The "Two Establishes" and "Two Upholds" political-loyalty language was prominent; safety-system language was absent.
  - **Source:** "Li Shangfu" — *Wikipedia* (citing the NPC Gazette and Xinhua) — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Li_Shangfu ("serious violation of discipline and law").
  - **Source:** "Li Yuchao" — *Wikipedia* (citing NPCSC bulletin) — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Li_Yuchao.
  - **Question IDs:** 1B.3 (negative — anti-corruption priority rather than safety priority), 8A.4, 8C.1.

### 8. One structural positive: rapid reconstitution of the C2 chain by year-end

## B. Net reading for lens 1B.3

The 2023 evidence is **strongly negative** for command-and-control discipline on Xi Jinping's watch:

- The nuclear-rocket force lost its commander, deputy, and political leadership in a single July 2023 sweep.
- The defense minister — who had just months earlier run the CMC Equipment Development Department that procures the nuclear arsenal — disappeared and was removed within two months of the PLARF purge.
- Replacements were drawn from outside the nuclear-rocket branch, an unusual step that the SCMP and Wikipedia both flagged as raising concerns about the security, credibility, and integrity of the PLA.
- No new public 2023 nuclear-safety, custody, or accident-prevention safeguard was announced.
- The official framing was anti-corruption discipline, not safety reform.
- The reconstitution of the chain by year-end (PLARF new command July; new defense minister December) is the one *modest positive*, but the absence of any safety-system reform narrative offsets it.

A strong ruler on this lens would have combined the anti-corruption campaign with explicit safety-system upgrades — a codified personnel-reliability program, custody-chain audits, organizational reforms separating anti-corruption work from operational readiness, and clear public communication about continuity of nuclear command. Xi did none of these in 2023.

**Net judgment: 1B.3 reads as a clear negative for 2023 — Xi weakened, rather than strengthened, command-and-control discipline at the top of the nuclear chain, even if final operational control of the arsenal was not at risk.**
